newsitem.title: UK: Music steals crown from comedy at Edinburgh Fringe.
newsitem.headline: Music steals crown from comedy at Edinburgh Fringe.

text.p: Music has finally stolen the crown from comedy at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival, which for the first time in years is swinging more to the sounds of latino and salsa than laughter.

A few years ago, stand-up comedy was being hailed as the "new rock 'n' roll" as recession-hit Britons drowned their sorrows in pubs and clubs in the company of manic or morose men wielding only a microphone.
But the number of comedy acts in the capital of fun has fallen this year from 256 to 221, while music -- be it classical, jazz or folk -- has soared from 261 acts to 320.
Some critics are already sounding the death knell for the "alternative" comedy of the early 1990s, which deemed no subject too taboo or too trivial to joke about.

Others say the era of the lone stand-up comic is giving way to a return to the kind of sketches and revues that in the Fringe of the 1960s proved a launchpad for the likes of Peter Cook, Dudley Moore, John Cleese and playwright Alan Bennett.
"I don't think it is the death of comedy," said Anna Arthur, spokeswoman for the coveted 16-year-old Perrier Fringe comedy award.
"I think there are a lot of budding comedians who are still developing their potential but who have simply chosen not to come up to Edinburgh," she said.

The best of the stand-up comics discovered on the Fringe in the past 10 years have long since given up their day jobs and some, like Eddie Izzard, Jo Brand and Jack Dee can now fill theatres for a month rather than play to a handful in smoke-filled pubs.

Others simply ran out of material, or found the public running out on them when many of their raunchier jokes had to be dropped to conform with the "family values" imposed by lucrative television deals.

"We've had a decade or more of witless meanderings from so-called alternative comedians," wrote Jack McLean of the Scotsman newspaper, rejoicing at the shrinking of the number of comedy acts at the festival.

"The talented few went on to become very straight indeed because they knew there was a limit to febrile dissertations on the content of the insides of their noses, and in the case of girls, a foul-mouthed exegesis on used tampons," McLean added.
Yet the Edinburgh Fringe is still a mecca for would-be comedy writers and performers as well as talent scouts.
London Weekend Television has set up a Fringe comedy writing award this year to reflect a shift towards more structured scripts and character-based invention.

"In the past there seems to have been a bit of prejudice against sketch shows. But this year there seems to be a real buzz about character-based revues," said Steve Pemberton, of the "League of Gentlemen" revue show.
Pemberton and actor friends Mark Gatiss, Reece Shearsmith and Jeremy Dyson leapt from obscurity a year ago to win their own radio series and a television spot for their quick-fire short sketches.

"We all come from an acting background so it is much more natural for us to develop and write about characters. Last year, from being unknowns, we were overwhelmed with agents and contacts. It is only the Edinburgh Fringe that can do that," said Pemberton.
